paragraphs: In those strange old times when fantastic dreams and the visions of madmen became part of everyday life, two people met at an appointed time and place. One was a lady with a graceful figure and a beautiful face, although she was pale and troubled. Something had blighted her too soon, at what should have been the fullest flowering of her life. The other was an ancient woman, poorly dressed and ugly, so withered, shrunken and feeble that even the time since she began to decay must have exceeded an ordinary human lifespan. No mortal could see them where they met. Three small hills stood close together. Between them lay a hollow, almost a perfect circle, two or three hundred feet across and so deep that a stately cedar would scarcely have risen above its sides. Dwarf pines grew thickly on the hills and partly fringed the outer rim of the hollow. Inside it were only the brown grass of October and, here and there, a tree trunk that had fallen long ago and lay rotting, with no green successor growing from its roots. One of these masses of decaying wood, once a majestic oak, lay close beside a pool of green, stagnant water at the bottom. Places like this, so ancient tradition tells us, were once the meeting grounds of an evil power and those who had sworn themselves to him. Here, at midnight or in the dim light before evening, they were said to stand around the scum-covered pool and stir its foul waters as they performed an unholy baptism. Now the cold beauty of an autumn sunset gilded the three hilltops, and a paler light slipped down their sides into the hollow.
“So, our pleasant meeting has come about,” said the old crone, “just as you wished. Tell me quickly what you want from me. We have only one short hour to stay here.”

As the withered old woman spoke, a smile glimmered across her face like lamplight on the wall of a tomb. The lady trembled and looked up towards the rim of the hollow, as though considering leaving without carrying out her purpose. But that was not to be.

“I am a stranger in this land, as you know,” she said at last. “Where I come from does not matter. But I have left people behind whose lives were closely bound to mine, and I am cut off from them for ever. There is a weight in my heart that I cannot shake off. I have come here to ask how they are.”

“And who here beside this green pool can bring you news from the ends of the earth?” cried the old woman, peering into the lady’s face. “You will not hear that news from my lips. But be brave, and your wish will be granted before daylight leaves that hilltop.”
“I will do as you ask, even if I die,” the lady replied desperately.
The old woman sat on the fallen tree trunk, threw back the hood that covered her grey hair, and beckoned her companion closer.
“Kneel down,” she said, “and lay your forehead on my knees.”

The lady hesitated for a moment, but the anxiety that had been smouldering in her for so long flared fiercely. As she knelt, the edge of her dress dipped into the pool. She laid her forehead on the old woman’s knees, and the old woman drew a cloak around her face, leaving her in darkness. Then she heard the muttered words of a prayer. In the middle of it, she started and tried to rise.

“Let me run away! Let me run and hide, so they cannot see me!” she cried. But then she remembered where she was and fell silent, still as death. Other voices seemed to mingle with the words of the prayer—voices familiar from infancy, never forgotten through all her wanderings and every change in her heart and fortunes. At first their words were faint and unclear, not as though coming from far away, but like the dim pages of a book we struggle to read in poor light that slowly grows brighter. As the prayer continued, the voices strengthened in just that way. At last the prayer ended, and the lady, still kneeling, could clearly hear an old man talking with a woman as broken and worn as he was. Yet these strangers did not seem to be standing in the hollow between the three hills. Their voices were enclosed and echoed by the walls of a room whose windows rattled in the breeze. The steady ticking of a clock, the crackling of a fire and the tinkling of embers falling into the ashes made the scene almost as vivid as if she could see it. The two old people sat beside a melancholy hearth. The man was quietly despairing, the woman tearful and complaining, and everything they said was full of sorrow. They spoke of a daughter, a wanderer whose whereabouts they did not know, carrying disgrace with her and leaving shame and suffering to bring their grey heads to the grave. They spoke, too, of another, more recent grief. But in the middle of their conversation, their voices seemed to melt into the sound of the wind sweeping mournfully through the autumn leaves. When the lady raised her eyes, she was there, kneeling in the hollow between the three hills.
“Those two old people have a weary, lonely time of it,” the old woman remarked, smiling into the lady’s face.
“Did you hear them too?” she exclaimed, an unbearable sense of humiliation overcoming her agony and fear.
“Yes, and there is more for us to hear,” the old woman replied. “So cover your face quickly.”

Again the withered hag poured out the monotonous words of a prayer that was never meant to find favour in heaven. Soon, in the pauses between her breaths, strange murmurings began to gather. They grew louder until they drowned and overpowered the spell that had called them up. Shrieks pierced the confused sounds, followed by the singing of sweet female voices. These gave way in turn to a wild roar of laughter, suddenly broken by groans and sobs. Together they made a ghastly confusion of terror, grief and merriment. Chains rattled. Harsh, stern voices uttered threats, and at their command came the sound of the whip. All these noises deepened and became more solid to the listener’s ear. She could distinguish every soft, dreamy note of love songs that, for no reason, faded into funeral hymns. She shuddered at anger that blazed up without provocation, like a flame catching by itself, and felt faint at the dreadful merriment raging miserably around her. In this wild scene, where uncontrolled passions collided in a drunken rush, there was one man’s solemn voice. Once, it might have been a strong, melodious voice. He walked back and forth without stopping, his footsteps sounding on the floor. Among the members of that frenzied company, each trapped in a world made entirely of their own burning thoughts, he sought someone to listen to the wrong he had suffered. He took their laughter and tears for the scorn or pity they offered him. He spoke of a woman’s faithlessness, of a wife who had broken her holiest vows, of a home and a heart left desolate. As he continued, the shouting, laughter, shrieking and sobbing rose together until they changed into the hollow, fitful, uneven sound of the wind struggling among the pines on those three lonely hills.
The lady looked up. There was the withered woman, smiling into her face.
“Would you have thought there could be such merry times in a madhouse?” the old woman asked.
“True, true!” the lady said to herself. “There is merriment inside its walls, but misery, misery outside.”
“Would you like to hear more?” the old woman asked.
“There is one other voice I would gladly hear again,” the lady replied faintly.
“Then quickly lay your head on my knees, so that you can leave before the hour is over.”

The golden skirts of daylight still lingered on the hills, but deep shadows hid the hollow and the pool, as though dark night were rising from them to spread across the world. Again the evil woman began to weave her spell. For a long time it went unanswered. Then the tolling of a bell slipped into the pauses between her words, like a sound that had travelled far across valleys and hills and was just about to die in the air. The lady shook against her companion’s knees when she heard that ominous sound. It grew stronger and sadder, deepening into a funeral bell tolling mournfully from some ivy-covered tower. It carried news of death and sorrow to the cottage, the great house and the lonely traveller, so that all might weep for the fate that awaited each of them in turn. Then came steady footsteps, passing slowly, slowly by, like mourners carrying a coffin. Their clothes trailed along the ground, so that the ear could measure the length of their sorrowful procession. The priest walked ahead, reading the burial service, the pages of his book rustling in the breeze. Although his was the only voice speaking aloud, there were also insults and curses, whispered but distinct, from women and men. They condemned the daughter who had broken her elderly parents’ hearts, the wife who had betrayed her husband’s trusting love, the mother who had sinned against natural affection and left her child to die. The sweeping sound of the funeral procession faded like a thin mist. The wind, which a moment before had seemed to shake the cloth covering the coffin, moaned sadly around the rim of the hollow between the three hills. But when the old woman stirred the kneeling lady, she did not lift her head.
“What a lovely hour’s entertainment this has been!” said the withered crone, chuckling to herself.
